findings.title: Hard-coded Slack token
findings.detail: A credential is written in the configuration file, readable by anything that can read the file and copied into backups and dotfile repositories.
findings.fix: Move it to the environment or a secret store and reference it (for example ${SLACK_BOT_TOKEN}); then rotate it, since it has been on disk.

findings.title: Credential embedded in the server URL
findings.detail: The URL itself grants access (path segment 2 (high-entropy)). Anyone who sees it can use the server: it is copied into logs, process lists, shell history, screenshots and support tickets.
findings.fix: Rotate the URL with the provider if it has been shared, keep the file private, and prefer a provider option that authenticates with a header referenced from the environment.

findings.title: Credential embedded in the server URL
findings.detail: The URL itself grants access (query api_key (token query key)). Anyone who sees it can use the server: it is copied into logs, process lists, shell history, screenshots and support tickets.
findings.fix: Rotate the URL with the provider if it has been shared, keep the file private, and prefer a provider option that authenticates with a header referenced from the environment.

findings.title: Literal value in secret-named field X-API-Key
findings.detail: The field's name says it holds a credential, and its value is written in the file rather than referenced.
findings.fix: Reference it from the environment (for example ${X_API_KEY}) and rotate it.

findings.title: Server runs with all permissions (Deno)
findings.detail: The server can reach far more than its tools need, which widens what a compromised or manipulated server can do.
findings.fix: Grant only the access the server needs (for Deno, --allow-net=<hosts>; for containers, a dedicated network).

notes: Tool descriptions, and the resources and prompts each server offers, were not checked: that needs starting the servers (sievant scan --inspect-tools, which runs them).
